text: Kliment Yefremovich Voroshilov (Ukrainian: Климент Охримович Ворошилов; Russian: Климент Ефремович Ворошилов), commonly known as Klim Voroshilov, was a prominent Soviet military officer and politician during the Stalin era (1924–1953). He was one of the original five Marshals of the Soviet Union, the second-highest military rank, junior only to the position of Generalissimo held by Joseph Stalin, and served as Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet, the nominal head of state, from 1953 to 1960. Born on 4 February 1881 in Verkhnyeye, Bakhmut uyezd, Yekaterinoslav Governorate, Russian Empire (now part of Lysychansk city in Luhansk Oblast, Ukraine), Voroshilov came from a working-class family; his father was a former soldier who worked as a railway worker or miner and experienced periods of unemployment. Voroshilov described a childhood marked by extreme hardship, beginning work at age six or seven, receiving frequent beatings from wealthy peasants, and growing up illiterate until enrolling at age 12 in a nearby village school, where he received two years of education. He became close friends with Semyon Ryzhkov during his school years. In 1896, he began working in a factory near his village, led a strike in 1899, and joined the Bolsheviks in 1903 at a German-owned factory in Luhansk (renamed Voroshilov during the Stalin era), where he led strikes during the 1905 revolution. In April 1906, he traveled to Stockholm for the Fourth Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party (RSDLP) under the pseudonym 'Volodya Antimekov' and shared a room with Josif Dzhugashvili, later known as Stalin. In spring 1907, he went to London for the Fifth RSDLP Congress, was arrested and deported to Arkhangelsk, escaped in December, and moved to Baku where Stalin was active. He was arrested again in 1908, released in 1912, and worked in an ordnance factory in Tsaritsyn (Stalingrad/Volgagrad). During the February Revolution, he was in Petrograd but returned to Luhansk, where he chaired the town soviet and was elected to the Constituent Assembly. His military career began in early 1918 when he commanded the Fifth Ukrainian Army, which was driven out of Ukraine by German forces; after a long retreat, his forces reached Tsaritsyn, where Stalin was posted as a party representative and Voroshilov was given command of the Tenth Army. Stalin and Voroshilov led the Red Army's defense of Tsaritsyn and sponsored the creation of the first Red Cavalry unit under Semyon Budyonny, composed mainly of southern Russian peasants. Voroshilov clashed with Leon Trotsky, who considered him undisciplined and threatened him with court martial in October 1918. He was later transferred to Ukraine as commander of the Kharkiv military district and then People's Commissar for War in the Ukraine soviet republic, where he supported the 'Military Opposition' opposing centralized army formation and the recruitment of former Tsarist officers. During the Polish–Soviet War, he served as political commissar with Budyonny’s First Cavalry. Voroshilov was elected to the Central Committee in 1921 and became commander of the North Caucasus military district in April 1921, then commander of the Moscow military district in March 1924. In 1925, after Mikhail Frunze's death, he was appointed People's Commissar for Military and Navy Affairs and Chairman of the Revolutionary Military Council of the USSR, a position he held until 1934. Despite holding high offices, he was not part of the inner leadership; in November 1930, Sergey Syrtsov alleged a "tiny group" excluding Voroshilov made decisions behind the Politburo. His key achievement during this period was relocating key Soviet war industries east of the Urals to allow strategic retreat while preserving manufacturing capacity. Frunze, aligned with the Troika (Zinoviev, Kamenev, Stalin), died in 1925 from a massive chloroform overdose during surgery, which Stalin's doctors urged despite previous advice to avoid it. Voroshilov became a full member of the Politburo in 1926 and remained until 1960. In 1934, he was appointed People's Commissar for Defence and in 1935 became a Marshal of the Soviet Union. During the first Moscow trials in August 1936, he signed the order denying clemency and ordering executions. He was a main speaker at the March 1937 Central Committee plenum, where he denounced Nikolai Bukharin and Alexei Rykov as "renegades." Initially, he believed the purges would not affect the armed forces and was unprepared for the arrests of Marshal Tukhachevsky and others in April and May. He openly stated that saboteurs in the Red Army were few and tried to save officers like Lukin and Sokolov-Strakhov, sometimes succeeding. On 30 May 1937, he ordered commander Iona Yakir to travel to Moscow for a Military Revolutionary Council meeting, knowing he would be arrested. At the June 1937 meeting, Voroshilov vacated the chair and apologized, saying he could not believe so many high-ranking officers were corrupt. Afterward, he played a central role in Stalin's Great Purge, denouncing military colleagues and subordinates when ordered by Stalin. He wrote personal letters to exiled officers like Mikhail Ostrovsky, urging them to return and falsely assuring them of no retribution. Voroshilov personally signed 185 documented execution lists, fourth among Soviet leaders after Molotov, Stalin, and Kaganovich. He denounced officers he disliked, such as Tukhachevsky. Despite purging "mechanisers" who supported tanks over cavalry, he believed cavalry use should decrease and modern arms should be prioritized. Budyonny tried to recruit him to protect cavalry, but Voroshilov openly opposed it. He praised the Red Army's combined arms capabilities and initiative during the 1936 summer maneuvers but also identified issues in the army, including poor communication, ineffective staffs, lack of inter-arm cooperation, and rudimentary command structures in tank units. After the purge, reforms were introduced to align doctrine with the army's actual state; Voroshilov and Kulik were among the instigators. However, they failed to implement these reforms effectively. One reform, the reorganization of field units, was conceived by Kulik and implemented by Voroshilov, which inadvertently moved the Red Army to a less advanced state than in 1936. Voroshilov noted that territorial units were disbanded due to their inability to train conscripts in modern technology. He had openly criticized the system as inadequate in an era of imperialist military expansion, and territorial units were unpopular with him and the Red Army leadership. These units were ineffective; conscript Alexey Grigorovich Maslov noted he never fired a shot during training, and real training occurred only once a year when veterans returned. Voroshilov commanded Soviet troops during the Winter War from November 1939 to January 1940, but due to poor planning and his incompetence as a general, the Red Army suffered about 320,000 casualties compared to 70,000 Finnish casualties. At Stalin’s dacha in Kuntsevo, Stalin shouted at Voroshilov for the losses; Voroshilov responded by blaming Stalin for eliminating the army’s best generals and smashed a food platter on the table—Nikita Khrushchev said this was the only time he witnessed such an outburst. Voroshilov was made the scapegoat for the Finnish campaign and replaced as Defense Commissar by Semyon Timoshenko, later being appointed Deputy Premier for cultural matters. Initially, he argued for the release of thousands of Polish officers captured in September 1939, but later signed the order for their execution in the Katyn massacre of 1940. Between 1941 and 1944, he was a member of the State Defense Committee. After the German invasion in June 1941, he commanded the short-lived Northwestern Direction (July to August 1941) and then the Leningrad Front from September 1941. Working with Andrei Zhdanov as German forces threatened to cut off Leningrad, he displayed personal bravery, including rallying retreating troops and personally leading a counter-attack against German tanks with only a pistol at Ivanovskoye. However, his counterattack style was outdated and drew contempt from military colleagues; he failed to prevent the German encirclement of Leningrad and was dismissed on 8 September 1941, replaced by Georgy Zhukov. Despite this, Stalin needed popular wartime figures, and Voroshilov remained an important figurehead. Between 1945 and 1947, he supervised the establishment of a socialist regime in postwar Hungary and attributed the poor performance of the Hungarian Communist Party in the October 1945 Budapest municipal elections to the presence of non-Hungarian leaders, claiming it was "detrimental to the party." In 1952, he was appointed a member of the Presidium of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Following Stalin’s death on 5 March 1953, Voroshilov was approved as Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet on 15 March 1953, with Nikita Khrushchev as First Secretary and Georgy Malenkov as Premier. Voroshilov, Malenkov, and Khrushchev jointly arrested Lavrenty Beria after Stalin’s death. As Chairman, Voroshilov oversaw death row appeals, presiding over meetings and having the most influential voice, though split votes were common and he was sometimes outvoted. He generally advocated leniency, especially for those showing repentance or convicted of crimes of passion or under the influence of alcohol, while judging political crimes and financial offenses more harshly. Many death sentences were commuted to prison terms during his tenure, and his successor, Brezhnev, adopted a harder line. The contrast between his relatively lenient appeals in the 1950s and his active role in the 1930s purges was noted by Khrushchev, who asked him, "So when were you acting according to your conscience, then or now?" After Khrushchev removed most Stalinists like Molotov and Malenkov from the party, Voroshilov’s influence declined. On 7 May 1960, the Supreme Soviet granted Voroshilov’s request for retirement and elected Leonid Brezhnev as chairman. Voroshilov died on 2 December 1969 at the age of 88.

Kliment Voroshilov influenced the committee to show leniency, particularly for those who expressed repentance in their appeal documents or were convicted of crimes of passion or under the influence of alcohol, while he imposed harsher sentences on those convicted of political crimes or acts with financial motives. During his tenure, many death sentences were commuted to prison terms of varying lengths. His successor, Brezhnev, took a noticeably harder line in appeals cases. The contrast between Voroshilov's magnanimous approach to pardons in the 1950s and his involvement in the deadly purges of the 1930s was noted even at the time by Khrushchev, who asked him, "So when were you acting according to your conscience, then or now?" After Khrushchev removed most Stalinists like Molotov and Malenkov from the party, Voroshilov's career declined. On 7 May 1960, the Supreme Soviet granted Voroshilov's request for retirement and elected Leonid Brezhnev chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Council. The Central Committee also relieved him of duties as a member of the Party Presidium on 16 July 1960. In October 1961, he was excluded from election to the Central Committee at the 22nd party congress. Following Khrushchev's fall, Brezhnev brought Voroshilov out of retirement and re-elected him to the Central Committee in 1966. Voroshilov was awarded a second medal of Hero of the Soviet Union in 1968. In a winter night in 1969, Voroshilov felt unwell and refused to call an ambulance; in the morning, he put on his military uniform, called a car, and went to the hospital himself, fully decorated. He died on 2 December at the age of 88 and was buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis, in one of the twelve individual tombs between the Lenin Mausoleum and the Kremlin wall. Voroshilov was married to Ekaterina Voroshilova, born Golda Gorbman, a Ukrainian Jew from Mardarovka; she changed her name upon converting to Orthodox Christianity to marry him. They met while both were exiled in Arkhangelsk, where Ekaterina was sent in 1906. While serving on the Tsaritsyn Front in 1918, where Ekaterina was helping orphans, they adopted a four-year-old orphan boy named Petya. They also adopted the children of Mikhail Frunze after his death in 1925. During Stalin's rule, they lived in the Kremlin at the Horse Guards. Molotov described Voroshilov in 1974 as "nice, but only in certain times," noting he always supported the party's political line because he was from the working class, a common man, a good orator, and clean, and personally devoted to Stalin, though his devotion was not strong. He actively advocated for Stalin, supported him in everything though not always certain, which affected their relationship. This complexity explains why Stalin treated him critically and did not invite him to private conversations, though he did come by himself, and Stalin frowned. Under Khrushchev, Voroshilov behaved badly. The Kliment Voroshilov (KV) series of tanks used in World War II was named after him. Two towns were named after him: Voroshilovsk in Donbas (now Alchevsk), Voroshilovgrad in Ukraine (now changed back to Luhansk), Voroshilov in the Soviet Far East (now renamed Ussuriysk after the Ussuri river), and the General Staff Academy in Moscow. Stavropol was called Voroshilovsk from 1935 to 1943.
